utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Dennis Lazarus from Mexico who has been with our team since November 2013 and holds a degree in international relations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Good morning, Mr. Radetic. Shall we continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, for the interpreters and for the court record, we need to ensure today that we both do not speak at the same time, and my apologies to the interpreters and to the court reporter for the overlapping speakers yesterday. Secondly, I wish to follow up on a couple of things that you said yesterday. At transcript page 45673, you said that the command of the 43rd Motorised Brigade moved to Kozara Putevi building sometime in late May and June. And Kozara Putevi is that building -- the military barracks across from the Keraterm camp. Did you ever go to that barracks building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building of Kozara Putevi? Yes, I did go there several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During the time that you worked at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that while I was at Keraterm the command of the 43rd Brigade was at Kozara Putevi. I believe that they were transferred there only thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that the unit remained at the old Zarko Zgonjanin Barracks, and that's Z-g-o-n-j-a-n-i-n Barracks. For the Court, this location is shown on Exhibit P03533. The unit that you mentioned yesterday is the military police unit; is it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember it well, you asked me about the command of the 43rd Brigade and you asked me where they were transferred to the Kozara Putevi building. This is what I answered: The command of the 43rd Brigade - and only the command - was transferred to the Kozara Putevi building. I don't know anything about the percentages, but I would say that I'm -- a vast majority of the troops remained in the Zarko Zgonjanin Barracks, and I'm referring to the 43rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, we have a lot to cover today in very, very limited time. I thought my question was clear. You said yesterday that the command moved from Zarko Zgonjanin Barracks to Kozara Putevi. You also said that the unit remained in the old barracks. I was simply asking you this morning to define what you meant by "the unit." Did you mean the military police unit remained at the old barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the military police, one part of the military police unit remained in the old barracks and the other part was moved to the white building behind the Keraterm building that I showed to you yesterday when you showed me that photo. But I don't know the exact dates when those things happened. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't know what it is about. Do you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to interpret 3533. We can see a building there, but you can't see the relationship of that building with any other buildings. And now the reference has been made to that relationship, so I don't know how to interpret that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was -- it was me noting for the Court that the Zarko Zgonjanin Barracks is simply located on that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue. I think that's okay. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, you said at transcript page 45683 that Dusko Knezevic was tried for war crimes and is serving his sentence. You're aware of the fact that he was actually tried in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a result of the transfer of the ICTY indictment to the Bosnian state court? You're aware of that fact, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusko Kraljevic is the name I heard yesterday for the first time. I don't know who you're talking about. As far as I can remember, Dusko Kraljevic did not exist in the 43rd Brigade, or at least I didn't know any such person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, yesterday I mentioned Dusko Knezevic who was involved in crimes --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- with Zoran Zigic. Now, you know that he was tried in Bosnia as a result of an indictment sent by the ICTY to the state court, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, for the transcript to be clear, in your previous question you asked me about Dusko Kraljevic, and now you just skipped that name and you're asking me about Zigic and Knezevic. Do we still need to talk about Dusko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, it's an issue of interpretation. There is a mistake in the course of interpretation. Please understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you able to answer the question, Mr. Radetic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question is about whom, Dusan Knezevic and Zoran Zigic, whether they what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm moving on. We're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I have Exhibit D04140 on the screen please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, will you please concentrate very carefully on my question and answer the question as succinctly as you possibly can, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you read the exhibit number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document you see on the screen is an official note signed by Dusko Sikirica, who is the commander of the Keraterm security, dated the 4th of July, 1992. And it states there that Zigic, an armed uniform person, together with Dusko Knezevic, Zoran Vokic, and Zeljko Timarac came to the Keraterm camp and beat prisoners to exhaustion and after which they would die a few days later. He asks there to the Prijedor police station number 2 to ask the responsible bodies to suggest to the military command that such conscripts should be prevented from committing these arbitrary acts. Now, Sikirica's statement about Zigic establishes that a crime has been committed, doesn't it? Can you answer that with a yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It arises from this now that the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Zigic and others as a result of this official note should have been arrested, should they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The police were duty-bound to inform the military command and the prosecutor of this 4th of July, 1992, letter, which contained information that crimes had been committed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, on the 4th of July, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there were neither a military prosecutor nor a military court. As far as I can remember, the military court and the military prosecutor's office were set up either at the end of September or the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: They could have informed the civilian police -- they could have informed the -- the civilian prosecutor, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Because Zoran Zigic was not a military conscript, nor was he a member of the 43rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, there was -- there was a military police unit under the military command of which you were a member, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so the police were duty-bound to inform the military command of this letter, and it was the responsibility, was it not, of the police and the military to investigate and -- investigate this matter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the military police was duty-bound to deal with illegal dealings carried out by uniformed personnel in the armed forces. Zoran Zigic was not a member of the military. He was not a military conscript. He could not even be mobilised because he had some health problems, as far as I can remember. The story about Zoran Zigic should have ended in proceedings carried out by the Ministry of the Interior because he was a civilian involved in the commission of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Dusko Knezevic, he was not a member of the military? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the unit of the 43rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: All right. We'll deal with some documents in a moment, but just before we do that, in paragraph 35 of your statement, it states that after 15 days at Keraterm you were assigned other duties. And in paragraph 33 of your statement, you say that you were transferred to the crime department of the military police. You said you investigated crimes against property and that 90 per cent of the cases involved Serb perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. There seems to have been some problem with your microphone. I'm not sure whether the witness heard your question in full. Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Whether I was transferred to the crime prevention service of the military police after a short while and the answer is yes, that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of your statement, you say that everyone who the military police found out had committed a crime was arrested and criminal reports were filed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was processed but that doesn't mean that he had to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- Mr. -- Mr. Radetic, you mentioned, you know, extensive looting, robberies. Now, the non-Serbs were the victims of these crimes - correct? --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Robberies --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- in the majority of cases?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A majority of those crimes were committed in the areas where there was no population and that's where looting and robberies happened. Those were the areas where combat had taken place previously, and I'm talking about 90 per cent of all the cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And those places where combat occurred where the civilians from that area were fleeing their houses, is that the areas that you're talking about, the non-Serb houses in the combat areas where the looting was occurring?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what about -- what about serious crimes? What about crimes against life and limb, war crimes against a civilian population? Did you investigate those crimes? You said everyone who the military police found out had committed a crime was arrested.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were processed. When it comes to crimes against life and limb, we had cases that could be processed. We gathered evidence. We investigated. We interrogated suspects. We collected evidence. We prepared documents for future processing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The focus was on property crime and not investigating crimes like murder and serious assaults committed against the non-Serb population, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot more crimes that pertained to property, at least according to the information available to the police, were known to the police. We did not know about the large number of killings of the non-Serbian population, and we knew about the others. We had information about those.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, you said yesterday that you informed your superior command of the crimes that you heard about -- oh, no, sorry, you informed your command about the crimes that you had heard about unofficially that had occurred at the Keraterm camp after you left. Now, there was no investigation by the military police into these crimes, was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, what about the room 3 massacre involving the death of over 150 detainees that occurred on the 24th of July, 1992, in the Keraterm camp? Did the military police investigate that matter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement that I provided to the Tribunal, I explained very clearly that during that period of time I was not in Prijedor. I was absent from Prijedor because my father was sick. After four or five days when I returned, I learnt about the killings that had occurred on the 24th of July. As far as I know in view of the fact that those victims were civilians and that the civilian police secured the camp, the police station in Prijedor was involved in some investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, wasn't -- wasn't -- wasn't it the talk of the town that a -- that a TO unit or a military unit was also involved in the commission of that massacre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned, I heard this: It was the talk of the town that some people tried to escape from Keraterm and that several of those who tried to escape were killed. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The unarmed civilians who were -- who were locked in a -- in a shed tried to escape and then they were machine gunned down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I was not there. I told you what I had heard and those were just talks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Let's turn briefly now to -- to the military court prosecutor's office. In paragraph 8 of your statement, you say that the main problem in the work of the military police was the fact that no military court had been established until September/October 1992 and there was no place to process the recorded perpetrators of crimes. We have evidence in this case that the military courts and military prosecutor's offices in the Republika Srpska were established much earlier and that was by a decision of Mr. Karadzic of the 31st of May, 1992, which is P03602. We also have evidence in this case showing that the Banja Luka military court was operational and functioning from August 1992, and the reference for the Court and the accused is Exhibit P03596. Now, the military prosecutor's office was functioning from at least mid-July, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-July I did go to the military prosecutor's office on business. A man was there in that room. He didn't have a desk. He did not even have a typewriter, let alone a computer. Captain Pisarevic, whose name I can't remember, was on the phone all day to try and get at least the bare necessities for his work. That's what the prosecutor's office looked like in mid-July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We have evidence in this case, Exhibit P03608 which shows -- which is the military court prosecutor's log-book, which shows that the prosecutor's office was operational from at least the 19th of July, 1992. But, Mr. Radetic, you were working in the prosecutor's office in -- in August 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of August, beginning of September. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were -- you were a desk officer or an administrative officer in the military prosecutor's office at that time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a professional associate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 25840, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, this is a cover page of a -- of a file for Zoran Zigic, and it's dated in the very top left-hand corner the 19th of August, 1992. And it's got a reference, 84/92. And if we go down to the bottom of the page, is that a reference to you down in the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that a reference to you, Mr. Radetic? That's being --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the answer is yes, but I cannot recall the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Well, you're the only --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're the only person with the surname Radetic that worked in the military prosecutor's office, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: How many pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's simply the cover page, one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Two pages in the English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6595, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you say in paragraph 7 of your statement that the civilian authorities, the police, and the army took measures within their purview against violators of public law and order and those who committed crimes and also in paragraph 8 that when -- as -- as we've just discussed, when everyone -- when you were working in the military police company, everyone was arrested but that you couldn't process them because there was no military court. You also said in paragraph 50 that attempts were made to process people who had committed crimes. But the fact of the matter is, Mr. Radetic, that the prosecutor's office and the court failed to follow through with prosecutions of perpetrators in relation to crimes committed against non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what actually -- are you asking me about the work of the military police or the military prosecutor's office? What is the aspect from which I should answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Military prosecutor's office and the court.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor's office, after it was enabled to do what it was supposed to do on the basis of the law, and that was at the end of September, worked on cases that it received from police organs to the extent to which these reports arrived and to the extent to which there was evidence supporting the reports. However, the focus of the military prosecutor's office in view of the war situation were problems within the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that rendered it impossible --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I said that the focus was not -- they didn't follow through on crimes that were committed against non-Serbs - that was my question - yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I cannot give a yes or no answer. I'd have to spend a lot of time to remember all of that. How could I possibly just say yes or no? I cannot recall how many such cases were dealt with as you have been referring to just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to look at an -- an example in the Prijedor basic court. Now, you worked there for seven years before the war, did you not, in the basic court?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we know that Zoran Zigic was arrested on the 1st of July and detained for three days for a crime of accepting bribery of 4.000 Deutschmarks from two non-Serb detainees in Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the reference for that is D01926. And the criminal report is D1925.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There is then a request by the Prijedor basic public prosecutor on the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can bring that document up, 25842, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, this is from Samba [phoen], deputy prosecutor, Drasko Zec. And it's addressed to the court, the investigating judge in the court, requesting to carry out an investigation against him and to detain him for one month for this -- for this crime of bribe taking. And it says on the 10th of June that he was a member of the unit providing security to the Keraterm collection centre. Now, we saw earlier the document P04041, the 4th of July letter written by Dusko Sikirica, the commander of the Keraterm camp, about the -- the crimes that had been committed by the four people named in that document. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was the -- it was the exhibit that we showed very early this morning, and it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Official Note written by Sikirica. Do you remember having seen that this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Of course. Well, this morning -- well, you know, I thought that you asked me whether I had seen that in 1992. 1992. In 1992, I did not see it or at least I do not recall seeing it. Of course I saw it this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I'm sorry if -- if there is some confusion, Mr. Radetic. So Mr. Zigic is arrested for this crime here in front of us, this -- this bribery crime. The very next day, after this letter is written to detain him for one month, Sikirica then writes and -- and informs the public -- the police station about the crimes being committed by Mr. Zigic. Now the police are duty-bound to hand that letter on to the prosecutor, are they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian prosecutor's office, yes. I assume the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now if we could call up 65 ter number 25836.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you ask any question about this request from the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was showing this to the witness to put it into -- to establish a chronology of -- of documents to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we see in front of us, Mr. Radetic, an undated letter, although it has a date stamped down in the bottom left-hand corner as having been received from the -- the prosecutor's office on the 8th of August -- 8th of July, I'm sorry. It's -- it's a letter of the sabotage reconnaissance unit of the military post 4777/3 Prijedor signed by Sergeant Dusko Knezevic, and it's sent to the public prosecutor, and it's requesting the release of the soldier Zoran Zigic accused of a crime under Article 230, saying because the unit will leave for Derventa and they -- they need Zigic because he's an exceptionally capable and disciplined soldier and one of the best explosive experts. Now, four days after the -- five days after the -- the document we just saw from the prosecutor's office asking for a -- for a -- for the detention for one month, we see Mr. -- where it -- sorry, where it says that Knezevic had been a member of the Keraterm security, which is attached to the police, we now see him being part of a military unit. And we have his partner in crime here, Dusko Knezevic, writing a letter for his release. Now, this military post, the sabotage reconnaissance unit military post 4777/3, this is a unit within the 43rd Brigade, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, could we have 65 ter number 25843 please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me. If the Prosecutor allows me -- or, rather, if the Court allows me, this document that is on the screen now and that was signed by Dusko Knezevic is a pure forgery. It's compiled by criminals in order to have one criminal help another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 25843, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is a decision signed by Zivko Dragosavljevic from the Prijedor lower court, dated the 9th --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Savljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- of July, 1992, immediately releasing the accused, Zoran Zigic. And it says -- it says here that he's fully admitted to having committed the crimes, and then says the reasons to keep him in custody don't exist anymore and also the public prosecutor's office proposed the release from custody. And then it refers to the letter written by Dusko Knezevic. Now, is this a legitimate basis to release when -- when Zigic has confessed to the crime and the matter could have gone straight to trial? But in any event, the -- the court should have been aware of the letter of the 4th of July, 1992, from Sikirica outlining that Zigic had committed a murder. And if the court had evidence that murder had been committed, he shouldn't have been released, should he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: As a professional, I don't like to state my views on the decisions of any court without having detailed insight into the case itself. Let me say this: As for this detention of Mr. Zigic's in that case and the constellation of the crimes that he had committed anyway and on account of which he was arrested, and so on, this is very mild, if I can put it that way, extortion, bribery. If Mr. Zigic admitted the commission of such a crime and if there was other supporting evidence before the court in addition to that confession, and it has to do with the crime of bribery, there would be no reason for detention on the basis of the Law on Criminal Procedure that was in force then and the one that is in force now. However, if, as you claim, the court had Dusko Sikirica's letter, then this is catastrophic, releasing Mr. Zigic from custody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 20 it was not recorded properly, "if."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, we understood that. You confirm that Mr. Radetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, I want to show you, you said you're not comfortable with dealing with -- looking at cases that you weren't involved in. Well, I want to show you some that you are aware of. You agree that this happened frequently, that the court was releasing perpetrators back to their units in order to replenish manpower at the front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a difficult question. That's a difficult question --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that cannot be given a general answer. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're saying it didn't happen frequently?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of "frequently" is a very broad one, and I don't know what the Prosecution means by "frequently."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: All right. I will be more specific. In relation to crimes committed by non-Serbs -- crimes committed by Serbs against non-Serbs, in those instances the court was releasing perpetrators back to their units, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall something like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been advised that my time is up, but I do wish to show Mr. Radetic four documents, if -- with Your Honours' leave. Sorry, five documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please conclude by 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, five weeks later Zigic was again involved in extortion. The previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant 10.00. Yes. Thank you for your indication, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I know I had asked for an additional half-hour, Your Honour. In my estimate -- my cross estimate was for two hours, but I will -- I will abide by the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, five weeks later Zigic is again involved in extortion. I mean, this one that we just dealt with was in relation to 2.500 Deutschmarks, but the next case in August dealt with an amount of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Did you mean to tender those three documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive them all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 25836 will be P6596; 65 ter number 25842 will be Exhibit P6597; and 65 ter number 25843 will be P6598.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now you know about this case, don't you, because the Banja Luka military court now dealt -- deals with this second case of extortion. And it's -- it's a case involving Zoran Zigic trying to get money from Husein Ganic, Husein Ganic. You know the case I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that individual case now. I know that Mr. Zigic several times tried or did commit crimes against the Ganic family. That I do remember. As far back as when I worked for the military police, that's when that kind of thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter number 25846, please. I'm sorry, 25845.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, this is a -- this is a decision signed Svetozar Davidovic against an appeal by Zigic rejecting it and keeping him in custody, because it concludes that he can repeat this same criminal activity and could influence the witnesses. Do you recall this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, Zoran Zigic was involved in 20 cases. When there was reasonable doubt. You see that this is August 1992. He was a suspect in so many cases. I really cannot recall all these individual situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter number 25846.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this document being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson? Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6599.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now this document is a decision in relation to Zigic's co-accused Mladen Dosen, and it actually is releasing him. And at the second-to-last paragraph on page 2 of the English, it says that the Chamber also weighed the need to deploy him to the same unit on the battle-field that he came from. So again we see these reasons about returning people to battle-fields.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are tendering this document, ask him a question whether he agrees with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you agree with what I've just said, that again this is another indication of courts releasing people back to their units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this exhibit, I cannot say anything because I don't know the essence. I'm not familiar with the case. This is one of the reasons based on by-laws that units needed soldiers. Now, releasing Mr. Dosen from detention, now, whether the court assessed all the reasons based on the law, if the reasons were not really there and he was released, then it's all right. But if there were reasons to keep him in detention, then what the prosecutor says would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6600, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit 25841, please -- 65 ter number 25841, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dosen -- Mr. Dosen -- Mr. Radetic, while that document's coming up, we saw a moment ago Mr. Zigic's appeal for release is -- Mr. -- he's kept in custody, that would be an opportunity to investigate Zigic for all the crimes that he's committed at the Keraterm and Omarska and even the Trnopolje camp which were known to the police and the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether keeping Mr. Zigic in detention was an opportunity to investigate other crimes that he had possibly committed, I don't think so because he was kept in custody because of a particular crime. The court and the prosecutor's office have a lot of work to do in order to prove the crime on account of which he is being kept in custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zigic appears before the military judiciary and the civilian judiciary in I don't know how many cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, we've already established that when you have evidence of a crime being committed, it should be investigated, especially when it's a crime of murder. While he was being detained on this charge, which related to 25.000 dollars, he could still have been investigated on the other crimes and additional crimes could have been bought, do you agree -- brought, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, at the prosecutor's office a criminal report arrives against a particular person. It is the authorised police institution that submits it. And in that report it says that -- and Marko Markovic committed such and such a crime and then there is a description. Do you really expect someone at the prosecutor's office when they receive this kind of criminal report that they address the police organ and say, Are there perhaps some other indications that this person did something else too?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, you testified yesterday that you told Majstrovic about crimes being comitted. You said the whole town knew about crimes being committed. They have an obligation to investigate these matters, the military police, the prosecutor's office. Surely that's the case. Now this document in front of us, 65 ter 25841, is a decision by Vojin Maric, of the 8th of October, 1992, releasing Zoran Zigic from custody. Now, Zigic was never tried for these crimes was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I think he was. I think he was prosecuted and convicted before a civilian lower court of Prijedor. I think it was on the charge of murder, but I cannot be sure because I was not involved in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He was --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exhibit P03608 shows that the -- that he file was transferred to the civilian court in 2000. He was never tried during the war. But he was arrested in June 1993 and tried and convicted for the killing of a Serb civilian woman named Danka Petkovic - you're aware of that, aren't you? - and he was sentenced to 16 years in prison?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In town he killed a woman, and I know there was a trial involving that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So he's in custody twice for crimes committed against non-Serbs, he's released on both occasions, he's -- commits an offence against a Serb victim, and he's tried and convicted and sentenced to 15 years in prison. That's the -- that's the -- the lot of it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot judge what's the lot of it out of three facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions. My time is up, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering the last document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6601, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency, thank you. Good morning, your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radetic. While we have this document before us, could you tell us -- first of all, look at the second paragraph of the explanation, the statement of reasons, in fact, where they suggest that his detention be terminated, and the charge requires psychiatric expertise from the centre where the detainee had been in treatment. Tell me, who was able to interfere with the judge's decision on custody?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are discussing this case and it's fresh in our minds, do you remember whether the criminal report dated 3rd July, 65 ter 25842 and now it has a P number, it was written on the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember who drafted the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the request to place in remand? I think it's the basic prosecutor's office in Prijedor that drafted that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Zigic writes his basic report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- whether this act by Sikirica is appropriate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to be precise. Shall we upload first Exhibit P6596? I'm not sure, did you refer to this, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, your Excellency, but it's good to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, let's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's good to have this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's upload first P25842 which was admitted as Exhibit P6596. So your question was about this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the request and was it sent on the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the case file, we see that it was typed up on the 3rd and I believe that from the reception stamp it's also the 3rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this document have to be proceeded by certain actions before the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The pre-investigating proceedings by the police forces, and the police then informed the prosecutor of all these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then on the 4th of July we see an Official Note written by Mr. Sikirica. What is the channel that this Official Note has to pass through and could it be before this request for custody?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't be before because it was written a day later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when this was already filed in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreter and the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how long does this Official Note have to travel and what is the road it has to travel to the desk of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The normal path would be for this Official Note by Dusko Sikirica to come first to the desk of the higher police officer to whom he sent it. This higher police officer when he receives such a document, gives it to the crime investigation police for them to check because very serious crimes are mentioned here. The crime investigation department of Prijedor municipality was supposed to carry out certain pre-investigating proceedings concerning these allegations to check if these are indeed true. After that with a criminal report against the persons named in this Official Note, they would approach the prosecutor's office in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you remember that the decision to release Zigic was finally issued on the 8th of October that year 1992. So if --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, no, that was the military court file -- the -- the civilian court file. He was released on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the 9th of July. And he was arrested again, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, he was arrested on the -- the 1st of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- and then released and then again around the 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So he was arrested and released at the end of the date on the 8th of October. So my question is: The report written by Sikirica should have arrived before the military court by that date, i.e., 8th of October 1992, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if there is any misunderstanding concerning this paragraph, this request to carry out an investigation was written on the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are talking about Sikirica's Official Note written on the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's D4140. It will come to your monitor soon. So my question again is that when the military court decided to release Zigic, it could have this document before it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Zigic was already released on the 9th of July and he was released by a civilian court, if I got the dates right, based on a letter that I said was a forgery, signed allegedly by Dusko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, so at that time that court may not have had that information originating from Sikirica, but by October it could have this information, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all the way up to 8 July we are talking about the civilian court of Prijedor, but in October there is a military court. I'm not sure that civilian police submitted and had the habit in practice of filing their documents with the military court as well. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we briefly look at P6595.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the lower bottom corner, what does it mean 24th August, then 26th August, and then the 7th of September? What are these additions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The lower bottom corner. Do you see these dates, 24th August and then some more additions? What does it mean, "additional investigation"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but these are individual documents made by the prosecutor's office and sent to various addresses from the police requesting them to run checks as well as other state agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Official Note by Sikirica, did you understand that Mr. Sikirica was in favour of such action or against it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He qualified them as perpetrators of the most heinous crimes. He was certainly not trying to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So such actions by Zigic and his accomplices, was that the rule or an exception?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously these were persons who constituted a glaring exception compared to the vast majority of the population of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This release from remand, does it mean termination of proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. Remand is just the most serious measure to ensure the presence of the accused, because it's contrary to basic human rights and freedoms. As soon as reasons for using this harshest measure ceases, it is terminated, and the investigating judge takes care all the time during the proceedings to make sure whether these reasons for the harshest measure are still present or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat his question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Karadzic, you need to repeat your question. Interpreters couldn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was: Which part of the reasons for remand custody is eliminated when an accused confesses guilt?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one reason that is eliminated is disturbance to the public. If that's the kind of crime that is charged, then even a confession does not eliminate reasons for remand in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radetic, did you have any knowledge that I, as president of the republic, come supreme commander, was interfering with the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. If you want me to be quite honest, when I was working in the military prosecutor's office, I really held a grudge against the president of the republic because he didn't give us more resources to work faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you connect these cases with the president of the republic? What does the president have to do with when somebody would be released from remand custody or detained, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president would be abusing his authority and office very seriously if he tried to interfere with live cases; that is to say, cases that are being processed by the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This Dusko Knezevic who wrote this letter --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at this document, by the way. It was 65 ter 25836 but now it has a P number. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from his signature, the signature of the person sending it, do we see any reception stamps? Do we see anything that makes this document trustworthy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the reception stamp of the prosecutor's office, and we see the number under which this was filed. I've looked at many documents describing all the things that these people had done, but this one I haven't seen. This was certainly a forgery. Mr. Zigic was unfit to be a member of the army. He was never mobilised for that reason and it's out of the question that he was part of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the same man mentioned in Sikirica's letter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same person, the same person who was involved together with him in these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was a bit of confusion about the location of the command and the location of the unit. Tell me, how far is Zarko Zgonjanin Barracks away from the unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not less than 3 or 4 kilometres. It's an entirely different part of town. It's on the Banja Luka-Prijedor main road, the unit, and the barracks is along the Prijedor-Dubica thoroughfare. Totally different roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radetic, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Radetic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the next witness is Mr. Torbica?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear his evidence after the break. But before we take a break, the Chamber is going to issue an oral ruling. The Chamber will now issue an oral ruling on the accused's "Motion to Reclassify Status of Intercept Exhibits," filed on the 17th January, 2014, in which the accused requests that the Chamber reclassify the status of 20 intercepts, which were previously "marked as not admitted" by the Chamber because it was not satisfied of their authenticity at that time. The accused submits that it has been the Chamber's practice to mark intercepts for identification pending authentication by "officials of the Croatian and Bosnian governments" and he intends to call such officials to testify in February 2014; therefore, to maintain consistency and avoid confusion, he argues that the intercepts should be reclassified as marked for identification. The Prosecution responded on the 20th of January, 2014, stating that it does not take a position on the accused's request; however, noting that changing the status of the intercepts at this stage of the proceedings is unnecessary as their current status does not prevent the accused from presenting further evidence which could ultimately lead to their admission. The Chamber first notes that the accused includes Exhibit D1787 and D2029 in the motion; however, both have been fully admitted into evidence. D2029 was admitted into evidence through Witness Vladimir Lukic on the 23rd of May, 2013. The Chamber further notes that D1787 was never marked as not admitted and, as noted by the Prosecution, the accused seems to refer to D1747 instead of D1787. As such, the Chamber will consider the accused's request to include D1747, not D1787. The Chamber notes that in its decision of the 7th of December, 2012, and the 7th of August, 2013, it marked the intercepts as not admitted because as a "special category" of evidence, intercepts may only be admitted into evidence if the Chamber is satisfied of their authenticity either after hearing from the relevant intercept operators or a participant in the conversations or after judicial notice of their authenticity has been taken, and the accused had not demonstrated either with respect to the intercepts. The Chamber considers that the status of "marked as not admitted" does not preclude the accused from making further submissions to demonstrate the authenticity of the intercepts, at which point, if satisfied, the Chamber will fully admit them into evidence. The Chamber therefore does not find it necessary to reclassify the status of the intercepts and thus denies the motion. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Torbica. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Torbica, before you commence your evidence I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Torbica. Straight away I would have to ask you, and I have to remind myself, that we should speak slowly and that we should make pauses between my questions and your answers. But first and foremost, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you provided a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9662.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement before you, Mr. Torbica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page and could he identify his signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you said to my Defence team or are there perhaps some errors that need to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes, whatever I stated is accurately reflected in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today as were put to you by members of my Defence team, would your answers in essence be the same as those in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: In essence they would be absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this statement be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning. No, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4228, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I'm going to read a short summary of Mr. Zdravko Torbica's statement in English. [In English] Zdravko Torbica was a member of the SJB Prijedor. He was involved in the war from the beginning, securing the railway lines and conducting traffic checks in border areas. He noticed that in late 1991 and early 1992 there was an increased number of buses transporting non-Serbs from Prijedor to Croatia and Slovenia. He was, therefore, aware that something was happening but was not aware of what and there was no proof of any weapons. However, Zdravko Torbica discovered the check-points when he was asked to accompany the ambulance carrying injured soldiers because the Green Berets had blocked the roads. Zdravko Torbica was on duty in SJB on 29th of May, 1992, when Prijedor town and SJB were attacked. The attack began with an explosion from the direction of the secondary school and the sound of infantry fire. Fire was not returned as the officers were not certain of the situation and indeed received orders not to return fire. The telephone lines were down and the only communication they had was via radio to the police station at Urije. The next day the soldiers were informed that the town had been attacked and there had been attempts to take over the building of the municipality as well as the SJB; once this situation was established, the order was given to defend the building. Due to the lack of communication, the officers were unable to warn their colleagues coming to start the next shift and a number of them were wounded in the cross-fire. One of the wounded officers was targeted from a house near the station and killed. Due to the heavy infantry fire, the officers were not able to help their colleagues. The perimeter of the MUP was guarded to stop members of the opposing forces from the entire -- from entering to the building. Assistance was provided by the police station at Urije; however, the vehicle they were travelling in also came under the heavy fire and a further police officers -- officer was injured. Military police arrived in addition to assist but were unable to enter the building. The firing stopped only when a tank arrived and stopped in front of the building. Five police officers were killed, one wounded, and eight soldiers were killed too. From April the 29th, 1992, until the June the 1st, 1992, 19 members of the Serb police and army were killed and 29 wounded by the Muslim forces. And now I would like to clarify several things live with Mr. Torbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Torbica, after the war did you undergo the certification process and were you certified, and, as a result of that, were you able to continue working in the police?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: After the end of war, my professional career continued in the police station for traffic safety in Prijedor until the year 2005 when I resigned because I wanted to be retired and I had all the conditions in place for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the war, who was it who checked the professionalism of our policemen? Who was it who was in charge of issuing certificates?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Immediately after the end of the war in 1997, members of the international forces arrived in my police station and they stayed there up to the moment when I was pensioned off. They were mentors in our police station and they checked and looked at every individual to see whether they satisfied all the conditions to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a member -- as a member of the traffic safety police, did you have an occasion to escort convoys? Did you know anything about the movement of convoys or the movement of civilians both of Serb and non-Serb ethnicity? Could you please tell us what you saw in that sense and what you were able to do?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: In 1991, one of the tasks of the police station was to escort vehicles who were over-sized as it were, including military vehicles, that moved through the area covered by my police station. In 1991, that happened very often. As from the civilian police sector, very often escorted such vehicles and those vehicles were wider and heavier than normal. They were always escorted by the civilian police, and the reason for that was safety of all the other participants in road traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the routes that those military vehicles travelled? Were those military vehicles and on what routes they moved?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I don't know why those vehicles travelled. Our task was to escort them through the areas that we covered in Prijedor. Whether they also took in -- went in other directions, for example, Banja Luka or the Republic of Croatia, I suppose they did. They went wherever they needed to go. They were mostly military vehicles. There were also other vehicles that escorted them under the law, but we escorted them and those transports obviously included convoys that moved in various directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about those convoys? Were they those convoys of civilians, did you know anything about the arrival of refugees from Croatia, did you know anything about departures from Prijedor, and did you play a role in all that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: First of all, all those things happened in 1991. My police station where I worked secured the railway line because we had been informed that the sabotage groups would blow it up, so we had to guard it during the night. After that, my police station was deployed on the border with the Republic of Croatia in Jasenovica and we stayed there until the moment when the bridge was blown up by the Croatian forces, and then we were moved in depth in Republika Srpska, and we stayed at that check-point for some time. I can't remember the dates. Our role at those check-points was to monitor the situation and the movement of people. We did not do anything with this regard. We only drafted Official Notes in order to inform our superior about any security developments. And when it comes to the escort of those military convoys, I personally participated in the escort of a tank convoy. I don't know what number it was. It moved from Banja Luka to Prijedor and its destination was the sports airfield in Prijedor. It stayed there for a short while in that area, and I know that people -- a certain number of people of other ethnic groups in Prijedor were not very happy about that convoy, and I know that a certain number of citizens who prevented state organs from doing their job were reported to the police, criminal reports were filed against them, and they included some police officers. I don't know how the whole thing ended up. I don't know what happened to those criminal reports. But I know that against some of the civilian population, including the president of the municipality, some police officers in Prijedor, criminal reports were filed but I don't know what the outcome of that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you to slow down to help the work of our interpreters. And now can you tell us -- or, rather, you say that the president of the municipality was involved in the incidents when the work of the military was obstructed. When was that and was it legal?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I believe that that happened sometime in 1991. Whether that was legal or lawful, I don't know. I suppose not because my colleagues from the crime prevention police deemed it necessary to file a criminal report against him. That's why I think that that gesture on their part was not lawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now could you tell us something about the year 1992. Did you know anything about the movement of civilians of non-Serb and Serb ethnicities -- or, rather, of Croatian and Muslim ethnicities? Was your public security station -- or, rather, your traffic control police involved in all that? Did you assist? Did you regulate something in that respect?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Whenever we received official requests in that respect, obviously my police station would meet such requests. Whoever thought that they needed assistance of traffic police, we extended that assistance. When I worked at that check-point that I spoke about, our only task was to control people who were interesting from the security point of view for our service and send reports and Official Notes. Those were the only actions that we were allowed and we did undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the police - not your police but -- because you regulated traffic. Did the police move people out? Did the police force somebody to form convoys and to move in the direction of Croatia, Slovenia, or Central Bosnia? According to what you know, how were those convoys formed? Who was it who requested from you to escort those convoys?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I don't know from where these requests came. In the morning when we would assume our duties, in our patrol orders for that day, we received specific tasks. I also don't know -- actually, I'm just talking about the traffic police now. I don't know that it exercised any kind of influence in terms of taking an adverse attitude towards other citizens of other ethnic backgrounds because our patrols were still mixed patrols at the time; that is to say, until the take-over and five or six days after that, in each and every patrol there would be a mixed composition, there would be one Serb and one Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on during 1992 when the war was already underway, did your service escort convoys? Who was in those convoys and which directions did they go to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes, my police station secured convoys in all directions. Now, who set what these directions would be and who channeled them, who said that they should go north, south, east, west, we really did not know. In my view it was done by the civilian authorities in the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity to help Croatian civilians from other parts of Bosnia to cross over a certain territory? Do you remember any such examples?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes. This was an order, a dispatch of yours that was sent to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. The Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska sent that further down to my police station, and I accepted -- or, actually, it wasn't that I accepted this, I was designated to be the escort of this civilian convoy throughout the territory of the Republika Srpska. This convoy involved citizens, women, children, the wounded, and other persons from the territory of Vares that was under the control of Muslim Croat forces. And this happened in 1993 when there was a conflict between the Muslim and Croat sides. I don't know on which basis but then you agreed on that; namely, that this convoy of civilians, women, children, should go throughout Republika Srpska to Livno. That is about 860 kilometres away. During that trip good and bad things happened, sad things, all sorts of things that can happen in life, but I am proud today to say 2.007 civilians, and I believe there were even more, arrived at their destination without a single negative gesture being involved, without any such thing happening in the territory of Republika Srpska. Although I had difficult problems to deal with, there were some people who were not under the control of the "armija" or the Army of Republika Srpska or the MUP. That happened to me at Romanija when I and my policemen protected these people with our own lives, lest they fall into the hands of these irresponsible people who were not under anybody's control. I remember that the leader of that group stopped me, asked who this was and what this was, generally, and I said that this was an order of the president of the state. And he said, Which state? And then I answered him, Well, I guess it's yours and mine. Then that person responded by saying that you were not his president and that you could not issue orders in the territory that is under his command. At that moment, there was a fierce showdown between my police that I commanded and this group that wanted to steal things from the people who were in this convoy. That was my assessment. At any rate, they didn't succeed in doing that. I was even wounded during that clash and it was only after that that I managed to go through all of Romanija with that convoy. We reached Sokolac, and then the assistant commander of the police station in Sokolac who was involved in traffic security, I told him about all of that and then he told me that there were many such groups in the territory of Romanija and that nobody could control them, the army or the police. Now this other gesture, this was something I experienced in Milici because this was a convoy of 72 vehicles. Some of them were buses, some of them were trucks. And then because of some of the obstacles that were on the road, the convoy was stopped. On the right-hand side, if you look at the way in which we were moving, on the other side there was also another large convoy that had been stopped and they were transporting soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I had a remarkable experience then. The soldiers from that other convoy, it was very difficult to do something like that and very risky at the time. The soldiers from that convoy were giving food to the people from the other convoy, these women and children. As for food and medicine in that convoy, there was very little of that, and my policemen told me that they had major problems on account of hunger. We tried to make do as far as water was concerned. When entering Banja Luka, I could establish radio contact with my superior command, and I asked for the problem of food and medicine to be resolved for these people in some way. The duty officers in Banja Luka told me that they would contact the Red Cross in Banja Luka and also the head of the operations duty service asked me to address Mr. Franjo Komarica directly in Banja Luka which is what I did. I left my deputy on the spot there and I went to the church in Banja Luka and I addressed Mr. Komarica and I explained to him what the situation was regarding these people in this convoy. After 10 or 15 minutes, I saw this wonderful image there. The Red Cross together with Caritas from Banja Luka gave enough food and medicine and water to these people, and that kept them going all the way to the separation line between Grahovo and Livno. Upon arriving in Livno, or, rather, the separation line, I had the hand over of this convoy together with members of the HVO, and today these people send me more greetings for my patron saint's day and other holidays than other people do, and I'm proud of having carried out this task that was ordered by you, Mr. Karadzic. And I and my policemen carried that out. To this day this is being referred to in the area as a major humanitarian achievement. I did not participate in any others but I heard that there were other such convoys when there was a conflict between the Muslims and the Croats. But on the basis of the contacts I had with my other colleagues who handled these other convoys, their experience was similar to what I had experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the beginning of Mr. Karadzic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please briefly respond to three questions: What was the ethnicity of these civilians; how long did this journey last; and Mr. Franjo Komarica, what was his function?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: This was only civilians of Croat ethnicity, 100 per cent. Franjo Komarica is the bishop of Banja Luka. And as far as I know, he is one of the main people in the Catholic church in Banja Luka. You asked me something else, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: How long this journey was? When the vehicles were taken in Livno and then travelling to Livno from Vares, this journey lasted for more than 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Torbica. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Torbica. Let me first ask you about your political background. You are a member of the SDS; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: When I ended my professional service -- I mean, I could not have been politically active when I was a member of the Ministry of the Interior. I said that in 2004 I was pensioned off, or, rather, I left the professional service. And from 2007, yes, that is right, I got involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In 1995, Mr. Karadzic awarded with a golden medal for bravery for all the efforts you took upon yourself during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes. Roughly in the proposal --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I appreciate short answer to the question. I think "yes" was enough, and then I'll show you one document and then I'll ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25824.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
