utterances.text: And what you're going to see on the screen is Mr. Karadzic's decree on decorations to the members of the Ministry of the Interior. And it says that: "To those who represent remarkable example, heroism ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we need now page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So here we will be able to see the title of the decoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And now we need the next page in B/C/S, page 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look item number 49, you should be able to see your name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question with a yes or no only, and for the following reasons --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Number 49.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But what are the relevant pages? Page 1 and page -- this page and the previous page. Three pages would be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you prefer excerpt, that's fine. But maybe you will be better assisted if you have all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have three pages at the moment. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P6602, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Torbica, you testified previously before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in two cases related to the events in Koricanske Stijene. In both cases you testified as a defence witness; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you told the truth to the court; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now we have -- we will focus a little bit on 1992. The SDS and Serb officials organised and implemented -- implemented the take-over of Prijedor which took place in late 1992; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: One of the steps the Serb authorities took in preparations for the take-over was to organise a reserve police; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Reserve police station. I didn't take part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 65 ter 18336.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a dispatch sent from Prijedor police station to the Banja Luka CSB in May 1992. It provides information on the structure of your police station. And if you look at the last paragraph, it says: "The new war structure, which is functioning now, was prepared during secret preparations for the take-over and it's ready to meet its obligations." So, Mr. Torbica, the take-over as well as the structure of the police station where you were working was prepared in advance and in secret; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: No, my police station, the one that I worked in, did not take part in the take-over. It was there like all the other police stations, but it did not play any role in the take-over of power. The structure in my police station remained the same just like before the war except for those policemen who had left our police stations. We took in reserve policemen so that we could carry out all our professional duties and have the right number of policemen in the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6603, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if we can have now P02968.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And with regard your statement just what you told us, that the police did not participate in the take-over. Now you will be able to see SJB Prijedor report on the work for the last nine months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we need page 2, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, could we just be precise. The witness is talking about a traffic control station. There should be no confusion. That's a separate station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Torbica, your traffic control section was within police Prijedor in town in the same building; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: It was not a section. It was a police station for traffic security under the direct control of the security services centre, Banja Luka, based in the police station; that is to say, the public security station of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you were under direct command of station Commander-in-Chief at that time? I'm talking about after the take-over. That's Simo Drljaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Perhaps only in the early days in the transition period. But Simo Drljaca in the public security station never had jurisdiction over the traffic security station because we fell directly under the security services centre of Banja Luka. With the establishment of the security services centre Prijedor in 1993, my station began to be under the security services centre of Prijedor, directly. But as long as we had a public security station in Prijedor, my station was under the direct control of the security services centre Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So from whom would you receive orders, from Drljaca in the police station Prijedor or someone from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: From the establishment of the security services centre Prijedor, all orders were received from Mr. Drljaca, and all orders concerning the traffic control station came from the CSB Banja Luka, the traffic security section.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In the document before, we can see it again, Drljaca says this is our police station, this is a structure, and he provides the information section on the traffic section.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We can have the document before back? That one was 65 ter 18336, item number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: He says, "The police" -- "There is a police station for road safety ..." and security. So this is within police station Prijedor. That's your difference to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Precisely. This document says exactly what I stated earlier. In Prijedor there is a traffic security station, not a section. And he only says here that it exists in Prijedor. I don't see anywhere in the document that he commands over that station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we have many other documents about the structure of the police. But let me ask you this: Regardless of your section, other police officers -- Serb police officers, they participated in the take-over of the power in Prijedor; that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes, except the police station for traffic security. And if you want me to describe its role, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following you, Mr. Torbica. Take a look at item number 8 in this document. It says: "The new war structure anticipates 13 police stations plus the police station for road safety and traffic control." It talks about, in total, 14 police stations. Are these stations not under the command of Drljaca at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My police station for road safety, he says 13 plus the station for road safety, makes 14. Now, what Mr. Drljaca meant when he wrote this, I don't know really. But organisationally speaking, what I'm saying is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And about the role of your section in 1992, you already told us about it this morning, but one of the tasks that your section was performing was manning check-points in Prijedor together with the military force; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And also as you were talking about at the time, people were deported from the municipality and your section assisted in this deportation; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was this said? Could we have a reference, please? When did the witness say that there had been deportations?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The witness was talking about the movement of convoys. So, in any event, this is my question to the witness about the deportation. He can answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Time-frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about deportations, but it is true that my police station - and I've stated this many times already - provided services of escort for transports. What does that imply? Physical security and traffic security are two separate things. Traffic security means that at the head of a convoy of ten or so vehicles, there is a police vehicle that will inform or let other vehicles in traffic of the convoy [as interpreted]. And it makes the transport safe in terms of rest time, in terms of speed, et cetera. That is what escort security means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And physical security of the convoy was provided by other members of the police station Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Physical security was provided by general stations; that is to say, the public security station of Prijedor except for the convoy that I described where both physical and traffic security was provided by the station for road safety and traffic control of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Another task of yours was a terrain search jointly with army members looking for unknown armed groups; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25812.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a CS -- SJB Prijedor report on a terrain search. If you see the name of the drafter or signatures, we see your name. This is your name; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It says the operation was carried with 30 policemen and about 20 VRS members. You took part in this operation; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Here in this document I see a typewritten name, but I also see this report was written by the sector leader. I was indeed sector leader and sector is one area within the area. Those are local and regional roads in the territory of Prijedor and the street network in Prijedor town. I haven't read the report. If you want me, I can read it and then comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's very simple. It's a report on a search of the terrain and it's drafted by you, and it says, including, among others things, that policemen and VRS took part in this. All I'm saying, this is your name and you took part in this; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I recognise it. I recognise this part of my report. It's true. I led the policemen via Ljubija to show them the way so they can enter this area because I had been in this area, but I didn't participate in the search of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Torbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6604, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: After the take-over, Mr. Torbica, many non-Serbs were brought to your police station for interrogations; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: No. Nobody was brought in for interrogation into my station. They were brought to the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate you trying to distinguish traffic section police and uniform police, but that's the same building. So you saw people coming and were being brought to the police station; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not trying to do anything. I'm just telling the truth about the distinction between the station for road safety and traffic control and the public security station. My office was on the third floor facing north, and the entrance door was in the middle of the building, and the auxiliary door leading into the compound was on the south side. So I could not see even physically what was going on on the lower floor because all my work took place in my own office. It didn't lead me to other offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence of non-Serbs being brought to the -- to the police station where they were beaten and interrogated, and after that transferred to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you knew this, Mr. Torbica, that people were brought to the police station being interrogated, being beaten; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: That people were brought in to the station, that much is true. I don't know why. I never witnessed any beating, especially because I never spent much time in the part of the building where people were brought in and questioned because that was not my job and it was not the job of any other policeman in the station for road safety and traffic control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 24, it seems the witness says, "I don't know why," and the witness actually said, "I don't know on what basis." Perhaps the distinction is not great, but it's more professional to say he doesn't know on what basis they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We could understand that. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25823.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these are notes of what a victim witness said during an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we need page 2, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The witness said that he was arrested in his apartment and brought to the police station. He said: "When I arrived, a policeman named Tomo took my personal details. One of the policemen, Zdravko Torbica, asked me what I was doing there and hit me in the head and stomach. They never told me why I was arrested. I was put in a cell, and there I saw Bato Deomic. From here, Bato and I were taken to Omarska." So, Mr. Torbica, the fact is you were involved in beatings of prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: That is not true. This gentleman you mention, Tomo, was indeed a member of the road safety station, but I don't remember I was ever present at such an event. Maybe you can show me the whole document. Maybe if I read the whole thing, perhaps I could recall something from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So you're denying that you beat anyone in the prison -- in the police station, actually, not prison; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: There is no citizen in the town of Prijedor or the municipality of Prijedor who could confirm today what is written in this document. I state this with full responsibility because I am not that kind of person. I am a professional policeman, a trained policeman, and I did not participate in any beatings, especially beatings of people who had nothing to do with my area and with my line of work. This man who is stating this, I don't know who he is, I don't know what he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's talk about your task of escorting convoys. You talked about escorting convoys of -- of military convoys. And, for example, if there is a convoy transporting any sensitive goods in your area of responsibility, you and your section would provide assistance to such transport; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I said at the beginning, we escorted convoys which were outsized or carried valuable cargo, anything that was required of the road safety station. We carried out all the orders, although it depended on who was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's say there was a crime site with a lot of human bodies that needed to be removed and transported to a burial site, so human bodies being transported, very sensitive transport. You and your section would provide assistance in such situation; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I did not participate in that and I never heard that the police station for road safety in Prijedor ever provided assistance of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Tomasica, a big mining site in Prijedor area; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Tomasica mine was used as a burial site for many hundreds of bodies of Muslims and Croats who were killed in Prijedor area in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I found out about that only when the mass grave in Tomasica was discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And your section assisted in escorting these transports to Tomasica; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I personally did not participate in such escorts. I don't know. And as far as I know, I think that my police station did not participate in escorts of such -- such ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25860.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is an article published in "Blic" in Serbia in November last year. And you already talked about Tomasica mine being exhumed. And this, what you're going to see on the screen, is one of many articles and news reports published regarding the ongoing exhumations at Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Could we zoom in, make this larger so I can read?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can zoom like the bold part and then later the first -- the paragraph at the bottom. But you will be able to see that in the first paragraph it talks about 430 remains have been exhumed so far, among which 275 complete bodies. And in the last paragraph on your page, it's second page in English, it says that among the documents that were found there are those belonging to people killed in Biscani on 20 July 1992. So, Mr. Torbica, you know about this site has been discovered and being exhumed as indicated in this article; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I've already said how I found out about the Tomasica location. When it was discovered and when it was reported by the media, I found out then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Prosecutor to specify: Does he claim that the entire number was killed in Biscani or it relates to only one family? I mean the citation of the words of one policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His question was this, it said this document says that: "... among the documents that were found there are those belonging to people killed in Biscani ..." I think that was fair enough. You can explore further, if necessary, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you would like to clarify, you may do so. Absolutely. Yes, please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And you were right, I was just referring what is in the article. I was not saying that this is 400 from Biscani. It's just what has been exhumed so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Torbica, this Chamber has also received evidence regarding the discussions that your chief, Simo Drljaca, had with VRS officers in 1993, during which they discussed Tomasica mine, where 5.000 Muslim bodies were buried and that the world knows about this from the released prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is in P1483, page 154, 155.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So having been reminded about the size and the scale of this clandestine burial facility for non-Serb bodies, do you still maintain that you, as a person responsible for the process of removal and transfer of sensitive -- sensitive transports, you somehow did not know about the hundreds, thousands of bodies buried at Tomasica or this, perhaps, information refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I never said that I was the person in charge of something like that. I don't know where you got that from. I was never responsible under any order whatsoever for such work that you are referring to, I was never personally made responsible for such things, and I never participated in such escorts. As far as knowledge is concerned, I didn't know because I was not at such a level of management as to attend collegium meetings that were attended by Simo Drljaca as well. I was not on that level. I was number four in my police station at the time. Ahead of me was the commander, then the deputy, then the assistant, and I was sector leader, number four.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So are you saying to us that you were not involved in this but your section might have been; is that you -- is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Torbica, you talked at length about escorting convoys, army, people, sensitive goods. Now we have massive burial, bodies, hundreds, thousands of bodies in mass grave, and now suddenly you say you don't know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: I was talking exclusively about what I did. This is my evidence, things that I participated in. And the patrol orders that were issued by the police station commander were issued to me in my name for each and every activity that had to be performed, and this is what I'm talking about, the only thing that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And your colleagues in other section of the police or perhaps in your section were involved in these activities; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: If I say something here, I have to know about those things. And if I repeat that I don't know and if I were to say that I knew something about that - and I don't - I'm a professional, I'm a policeman, I know that my every word has to be corroborated by evidence. I can't answer by saying that there were such things because I don't know. I was not involved. I was not involved in such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this article, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness doesn't -- hasn't confirmed anything about the article other than he heard -- he read about this event in the newspaper in 2013. This is not a proper basis for admission. And if this kind of evidence is important to the Prosecutor, they can make a motion to reopen their case and present it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The issue was simple, his knowledge about the Tomasica mine. And he said that he learned only from the media. And I put to him one of the articles that is published -- being published at the time, and he confirmed this is how he learned about this. So he confirmed the content of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's observation, and then I take it that your purpose has been accomplished by the transcript we have now. Shall we continue? We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Torbica, regarding the incident of 30th May, 1992, you say there was no communication at the police station except for one radio communication. You said the telephone lines were down. This is page 3 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have now 65 ter 25822.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a story published in "Kozarski Vjesnik" in 1993 about this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We need English page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in B/C/S, Mr. Torbica, if you look at the portion in second row just above the -- just above this paragraph that we see in the middle, which is the content of the conversation between Savo Golubovic and Cvetjko Rendic about this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If we can scroll down in B/C/S, a little bit down -- oh, sorry, then up. Still up. We need like the -- we need to see the -- further in the middle of the page. Further, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Torbica, you will see just above the paragraphs on your -- on your left side. There is a -- and it says, quote: "'Is there a telephone up there,' Rendic asked him while pointing at the Ribar. "'There is, but it's locked,' Savo replied. "The two of them somehow managed to run across to the Ribar, force the door, and get to the phone. Call the SUP. "'We're under attack, send help and ammunition,' Rendic said in a single breath. "'Most probably not a chance, because we're under attack here, too,' the duty officer informed him." Mr. Torbica, Ribar, Ribar is a restaurant in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Rendic was -- may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just -- let's hear him out. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rendic was at the check-point between Hotel Prijedor and the restaurant Ribar, which is about 800 metres away from the police station. I don't know what time of day is it in the morning, but at the moment when we wanted to inform our colleagues who were supposed to relieve us of duty, what to expect, we couldn't because the telephone lines were down at the moment. I'm talking about the time when we wanted to inform our colleagues not to enter and risk their lives. We wanted to save their lives. We could not inform them, and all four of them -- or, rather, all five of them were killed as they were on their way to work to relieve us who were on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So the telephone lines were -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So the telephone lines were working, Mr. Torbica, Savo and Cvetjko went to restaurant and called the SUP. It's not what he is saying that there was no -- that the lines were down.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO TORBICA
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that we could not inform our colleagues by telephone. Had we managed to inform them, they would still be alive today. How did Mr. Rendic contact the public security station and at what time? I don't know. At the end of the day, this is a newspaper article. This is not an official report. I don't know what this journalist wanted to say, what Rendic had told him. Whether he had told him the truth, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the Defence's non-opposition [Realtime transcript read in error "Defence not having a position"], we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6605, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Nothing further. Nothing further, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, your Excellency. No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript should read: "In light of the Defence's non-opposition," line 22. Yes, Mr. Torbica, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go. But we'll have a break for 45 minutes. We'll rise all together. We resume at 5 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you hear me in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Mandic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you and I have to remind myself that we should both speak slowly and that we should make pauses between my questions and your answers and vice versa so that everything may be recorded and that we may avoid any waste of time. As a result, the record will be clearer. Have you provided a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 1D9661.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the left side of the screen. Do you see your statement in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now do you -- uh-huh. And now can you look at it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could you tell us whether you have read this statement and whether you've signed it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation and I'm asking the same of you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the last page where he will be able to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this indeed your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you told my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today in the courtroom, would your answers in a sense be the same as in this statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm tendering this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No objections. I just would like to put on the record a remark about the leading nature of some of the questions that were asked which have been provided in the statement. So, for example, question 11 where the witness was asked after the failed attack on Prijedor town: "Why did the Muslims want to leave?" Which, in a case where expulsions form such an essential part of the allegations, it's obviously inappropriately leading. Questions 18 and 19 are similarly problematic. This, in our submission, goes to the weight that the answers should be given. And in light of the mounting pattern of similar problems, this goes to the weight that should be attributed generally to Defence Rule 92 ter statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'm going to read a short summary of Mr. Bosko Mandic's statement in English. [In English] Bosko Mandic was a member of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality in 1992. On 16th of April, 1992, he was appointed deputy president of the Executive Board of the municipal assembly of Prijedor. After Slovenia and Croatia seceded from the SFRY and after the plebiscite for BH and the formation of the HDZ and SDA, the Serbian people realised that they had to get organised politically in order to avoid the suffering of World War II be repeated. After 9th of January, 1992, with the establishment of the Republika Srpska Assembly, the Prijedor Serbian Assembly was also established. Following the peaceful take-over of power in Prijedor on 30th of May, 1992, the National Defence Council made a decision that a crisis staff be established in order to more easily overcome the new, complex political, and security situation in the territory of Prijedor municipality. Nobody from the authorities at the time organised or instigated the removal of the non-Serb population. However, a large mass of the non-Serbian population felt economically, financially, and generally unsafe after the political and security situation in BH became complex and started leaving the municipality. The people leaving were mainly women, children, and elderly, with the able-bodied men staying behind. The first incident in the territory of Prijedor municipality happened on 22nd of May, 1992, when Croatian and Serbian soldiers were stopped and killed at the check-point in Hambarine by Muslim paramilitary forces. After various unfruitful attempts to peacefully resolve the situation, the Prijedor Crisis Staff issued an order to the police and army forces to remove the check-point in Hambarine and to bring the killers of the soldiers to justice. At the same time, the political and military leadership of Prijedor municipality started negotiations with the representatives of the Kozarac Territorial Defence in order to establish normal traffic on the Prijedor-Banja Luka road. Civilians who did not wish to participate in the conflicts with the Serbs were accepted and kept in the town of Prijedor and Trnopolje camp for their own safety until a decision was made on whether they should leave or stay. At the same time, Muslim paramilitary forces fled to the woods of the Kozara mountain and organised occasional incursions into the neighbouring villages of Bozici, Lamovita, and Babici during which they massacred Serbian civilians in those villages. After the attack on Prijedor on 30th of May, 1992, the majority of the Muslims extremists decided to flee to other countries. All those non-Serbs who did not violate the law and did not possess weapons also decided to leave Prijedor town and were helped by the local authorities during this process. Their departure was made possible and organised through the Red Cross in Prijedor and International Red Cross. Those people who participated in combat or had been captured with weapons were taken to the Omarska investigation centre and their criminal responsibility was determined. At the same time, a huge number of Serbian refugees from Croatia and from other towns in BH under Muslim and Croatian role, they arrived in Prijedor looking for accommodation. The Prijedor Crisis Staff, through its regional staffs, accepted and registered the refugees and temporarily accommodated them in abandoned houses and apartments. The paramilitary formations which belonged to the Muslim and Croatian forces caused conflicts and incidents in the territory of Prijedor municipality. Some of the Serbian villages were stormed, the houses were torched, and the civilians killed. As for the paramilitary formations on the Serbian side, all people who were exempt of military service or declared unfit were to return weapons. There were problems of communication with the central authorities and the systems were down for an extended period of time. The civil war that broke out in BH was the result of centuries-long animosity, hatred, and revenge, and if murders or incidents happened, they could only have been perpetrated by individuals or groups which the authorities were unable to place under control. And I -- at that moment, I do not have additional questions for Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Mandic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing; that is, through your written statement here. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 7 of your statement you talk about the take-over of power in Prijedor and you state that that was on the 30th of May, 1992. The evidence in this case indicates that that was -- that that take-over occurred on the 30th of April, 1992. Do you accept that the take-over in fact took place on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And one more thing, if I may be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 5 it says that Mr. Karadzic said the vice-president of the Executive Board, whereas Mr. Karadzic actually said "the deputy president," and I would like to correct that. The two things are different. I don't want those two things to clash. That's on page 1, paragraph 5. Mr. Karadzic said that I was the deputy president because the deputy president is something different than the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The deputy prime minister of the municipality, as a matter of fact that should be really "vice-president."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following that, but I leave it there. I'll leave it to the parties to clarify further. Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that, Mr. Mandic, you confirm that paragraph 5 of your statement is correct: You were the vice-president of the Executive Committee of the Serb --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- municipality? Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now back to the take-over on the 30th of April. At paragraph 23 you describe that take-over as a reaction to the telegram received on the 29th of April. But, in fact, it's true, is it not, that the Serb authorities in Prijedor had been preparing that take-over long before the 29th of April and that telex was simply a trigger that accelerated the timing of something that had long been in preparation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Shall I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were aware of the time that we lived in. We were aware of our history before that, and we knew that representatives of the SDA party had decided to take over entire Bosnia-Herzegovina and what happened to the Serbian people in the Second World War was supposed to happen to them again in the new war. Those who were born, they have a family history where their uncles and fathers paid with their lives, so we had to prevent anybody from doing that again. We wanted to avoid that danger, but we wanted to do it without bloodshed or any new traumatic events.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you agree, then, that the Prijedor SDS was preparing the take-over of power in Prijedor long before receiving the telex on the 29th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: We had to organise ourselves in one way or another through meetings, talks, negotiations, but it was done to a lesser extent than the SDA and terrorists who were prepared to do everything. And you can see from the moment when power was taken over that nobody faired badly, nobody was wanting anything, either material goods or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we can go to P2968, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, this is a Prijedor SJB report for the -- the last nine months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph, the report refers to the circumstances where it claims ethnic maps were being drafted which placed Prijedor in the Cazin Krajina. Activities were launched to prepare for a take-over by force. These activities gained momentum in April, and the actual date of the take-over was forced upon us by the presidency. And it refers to the contents of the telex that you also refer to in your statement. And then it says: "As a result in the night between 29 and 30 April, 1992, following very detailed preparations and pursuant to the relevant decision of the Executive Committee of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor, an organised take-over of power was embarked upon." And it goes on to discuss the role of 400 policemen in carrying out that take-over. Now as this police report makes clear, this take-over by the SDS in Prijedor was planned long before the telex was received on the 29th of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that was not the only reason. I mean, the Cazin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now you talk in your statement about events in Hambarine in late May. This is at paragraph 10 of your statement. And you refer to the check-point incident in Hambarine. And you said that the Prijedor Crisis Staff called for the Muslim extremists to hand over the bodies of the killed soldiers and those responsible for their killing, and called again the next day for the citizens of Hambarine to hand over the alleged perpetrators of this incident. Now, the truth is, Mr. Mandic, this call by the Crisis Staff was in the form of an ultimatum, wasn't it? In other words, the Crisis Staff instructed the population of Hambarine to hand over the alleged perpetrators and said that if the ultimatum was not obeyed, the Crisis Staff was no longer willing or able to guarantee the safety of the civilian population; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. It was actually not an ultimatum because a lot of time was left to them to think and to hand over the bodies or -- and the wounded and to hand over the extremists who were the perpetrators of those crimes. You know, killing a man is a big thing and it was said clear and loud on Radio Prijedor that children and the elderly should seek shelter because we were prepared to carry out an action that would allow us to get hold of the bodies and those who committed the crime. And it was not done on the day when the incident happened but on the following day because those were not only Serb soldiers, they were JNA soldiers, but not only Serbs but also Croats who got killed. So it was not an ethnic thing or a mono-ethnic thing on account of which somebody could say it was just Serbs trying to protect their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, I didn't ask you anything about ethnicity and my time is very limited, so I would like to ask you to focus very much on the precise question that I'm asking and limit your answer to the -- to that question. You said in response to my question: Yes, that's how it was. But then you say that it was not an ultimatum. You agreed, do you not, that the Crisis Staff told the population to hand over the alleged perpetrators, and if not, the Crisis Staff was no longer willing or able to guarantee the safety of the population. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, no, we asked those who did that to surrender. We didn't ask the population to surrender; that is to say, that those who committed this crime were supposed to surrender. There is Mirza Mujadzic there, and it is well known who led the SDA and who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we got translation for the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That the perpetrators, that is to say the participants of this crime, be brought to justice, that they be prosecuted for what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have P3485, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic in the top right-hand corner of this page of "Kozarski Vjesnik," there are a number of public statements of the Crisis Staff reproduced, and I would like to direct you to the very top right corner of this page which reproduces a Crisis Staff statement of the 23rd of May, 1992. And at the very end, the last two paragraphs of this statement, says that the Crisis Staff orders the population of Hambarine and other local communes in the area to hand over the perpetrators of this crime - they were talking about the check-point incident - by the same day at noon. And the last paragraph says: "This crime has exhausted all dead-lines and promises, and the Crisis Staff no longer can, nor is willing to, guarantee the safety of the population of the above-mentioned villages in this area." That was the message of the Prijedor Crisis Staff to the population of Hambarine, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: If this is the original text provided by the Crisis Staff, that means that everything had been exhausted and the Crisis Staff asked for this to be brought to an end and that the perpetrators of this crime be brought to justice. So obviously the population sided with their heros and they did not do a single thing in order to hand them over to the authorities. However, this same population had already fled from Hambarine and they did not wait for the army or the police, only the extremists.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And now you said that on the 23rd of May the police and the army carried out an action in Hambarine, and by the evening the operation was over. You claim that there was strong resistance to this action by the Muslim extremists. In fact, the army suffered no casualties in this operation, did it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me, who suffered casualties. It didn't really reach me and I did not have this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, if we could stay on this document and go to the next page in the English and move down -- zoom out a little in the B/C/S and move down slightly. So that -- I'm looking now at the Crisis Staff statement of the 24th of May, 1992, which you can see is in this inner box --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Exactly, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is a Crisis Staff statement from the following day, the 24th of May, and in the first paragraph, this is just under the line in the English, at its morning session the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff discussed the situation in the municipality, and it says: "Following yesterday's operations by the army directed as disarming the Muslim paramilitary formations from the Hambarine local commune, the situation had calmed down during the night. The Crisis Staff assessed that the operation has been successful. The army suffered no loss during the combat activities. One member was wounded." Now, a moment ago you said you didn't have this kind of information. Does this remind you that, in fact, the Crisis Staff did the following day know that the army had suffered no casualties in the Hambarine operation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. It's been over 20 years now. Whether there were any wounded or not, I cannot remember. Maybe I didn't attend the session, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement you describe this operation as -- as one that was undertaken to remove the check-point in Hambarine and locate the alleged perpetrators of the check-point incident. The fact is, Mr. Mandic, that the entire village was shelled, wasn't it? That was the army's response to this check-point incident, to shell the village.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have that information. I cannot remember that detail. I did not take part in these attacks, so -- I mean, had I participated I would have known, but I did not participate and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: How about the shelling of Kozarac for two days, do you remember that? A couple of days after Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Believe me, my work did not really have anything to do with the police or the military. Maybe. I don't know. If you find the text, maybe it would be there. I really don't know. I didn't really deal with that, so -- I mean, I was a member of the Crisis Staff, but I did not follow what the army and the police were doing. That is their own line of work, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, did you ever have occasion to travel the Prijedor-Banja Luka main road from where you could actually see the destruction of the houses in Kozarac? Could you see those destroyed houses?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Not then. I didn't travel at all. Until these things happened, perhaps I was in Banja Luka once or twice. But when the operation was over, I went to Banja Luka. You know, there was no need for me to travel. You see, there was the president of the municipality and others who were supposed to co-operate with the autonomous region of the Krajina. There was no need for me to do that, so I did not travel therefore.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 10, you state that Trnopolje was set up -- was set up and that civilians were kept there for their own safety until a decision was made on whether they would leave or stay or until they obtained documents to go to third countries. Now, the civilians in Trnopolje were not there by choice, were they? They had been detained by the police and the army and they were held in Trnopolje as detainees; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, it's not right. I think it would have been better for the civilians to be in Trnopolje protected rather than in the street where some fool in uniform could walk up and make trouble. So they were free to enter Trnopolje and leave Trnopolje. In fact, they sought protection. They wanted to spend the nights in Trnopolje and during the day they would go home. The aim was to protect them because I myself, as a Serb, I was afraid. I was afraid of people with weapons. I wasn't afraid of Muslims or Croats. I was afraid of my own. I'm referring to those who were shooting at random, who were getting drunk and creating trouble in Prijedor. May I go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, you've answered my question, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said that the Muslims sought shelter in Trnopolje and you say that the Serbs -- you, yourself, as a Serb was also afraid. But there were no Serbs seeking shelter in Trnopolje, were there? It was just Muslims and Croats, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there were any Serbs. Believe me, I did not carry out any kind of triage and I don't have any information about that. I'm just saying that I was afraid. I as a Serb who lived and worked there. I was afraid of people who were shooting at random, who were drunk, things like that. Such a person would turn a rifle at me as well, not only a Muslim. They would no longer know who was who. And it's better for people to be protected rather than be left at the mercy of those who took advantage of the situation, killed people, and so on. There was a war going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have P2915, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is a list of -- summarising conclusions adopted by the Executive Committee and by the Crisis Staff. The list of conclusions adopted by the Crisis Staff begins about halfway down the page and continues.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in both languages. Towards about two-thirds of the way down in the English and the second full entry in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It refers to a conclusion of the Crisis Staff of the 2nd of July, 1992, forbidding the individual release of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm. Now, it's clear from the title of this decision that the people in Trnopolje were detained there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was temporary, I think. Precisely so they would not go back, because it was possible that there was this area where there were moping-up operations against terrorists, and then perhaps there were land-mines left in some of these houses. So I think that that was the idea, that they should not go home because they might get killed, not by the army or the police but those who were still there, who were not arrested, who had weapons, and also until people would see how these persons who had requested to leave could be safely transported to third countries because they had expressed a wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 12, you speak about Omarska and you say that people who participated in combat or were captured with weapons were taken to Omarska where an investigation was conducted and criminal responsibility was determined. This is a claim you repeat again at paragraph 20. The truth is, Mr. Mandic, that Omarska was full of non-Serbs who had had nothing to do with combat or weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Could you please show me that? Which paragraph was it that you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said this twice in your statement at paragraph 12 and again at paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Why was that done? Obviously because in the field in Omarska there were many inhabitants -- or, rather, those people who had weapons. But there were also those who did not have weapons. If there were few rifles, then there would be a second or a third person waiting in line to take over that weapon. I was not in Omarska until last year. Simply, it was not my line of work, but I assume that they all had to go through this triage -- or, rather, there were these organs who were interrogating people, asking whether they had taken part in this armament, and now they were either released or transferred to the collection centre of Trnopolje. I don't know. I have not really followed this because I think that there were many people there in uniform, and even apart from that you had to carry out a triage. You could not determine out in the field and say, You did shoot, you did not shoot.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the Prijedor SJB acknowledged officially that there were people in Omarska who "were not interesting from a security point of view, but who were captured because they found themselves in combat zones," and people, "for whom there was no substantial proof that they had participated in the armed rebellion in any manner whatsoever."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's D470 at page 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Were you aware of this assessment by the Prijedor SJB, a body largely responsible for detaining and processing these detainees?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, if that's what they wrote, then that's the way it was. But I think there were non-Serbs -- or, rather, there were Serbs who were there also, Igor Kondic, I know that myself. How he happened to be there, I don't know. I did not carry out a triage. I did not interrogate anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 28 of your statement, Mr. Mandic, you comment on some adjudicated facts regarding dismissals of non-Serbs, particularly from leadership positions in Prijedor. And you said that leaving a position of authority depended on one's respect for the constitution and laws and not on nationality. If a person of any nationality was loyal to the state, he or she would remain in position. The Crisis Staff, Mr. Mandic, of Prijedor issued an order requiring that certain posts considered to be important could only be held by ethnic Serbs, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which places they were, believe me; for example, what is important is the public security station and there were Muslims among the ranks of the police there. Also, at the post office there were both Muslims and Serbs working there and Croats, too, and there were directors, that is to say, top people heading companies. For example, GIK Mrakovica, I think that the gentleman's name was Bilo Begovic, and he was the director there and nobody touched him because he did not co-operate with the extremists and he was loyal, a loyal citizen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, you didn't really answer my question. You were a member of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. The Crisis Staff issued an order that only ethnic Serbs could hold certain posts that were considered important. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I think that that is not the way it was. I think that they had to be loyal citizens according to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P2740, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, you can see that this is a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff of the 22nd of June, 1992. And under point 1, you can see that the decision requires that only personnel of Serbian ethnicity may hold executive posts, posts where the information flow is possible and posts involving the protection of socially owned property; that is, all posts of importance for the functioning of economic entities. And it states that this includes all socially owned enterprises, shareholding societies, state institutions, public enterprises, the MUP, and the army. Now, the Prijedor Crisis Staff received this decision and forwarded it for implementation; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness start his answer again? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that I didn't have to accept that. I mean, if they were loyal, the leading people who were Muslims and Croats. I mean, quite simply we did not resolve that problem on the basis of the decision of the AR Krajina. If this information defines these enterprises that were important, then it must have been that. But when we assess that there was no need to replace people, then we wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you recall receiving this decision, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I did not have any contact with the AR Krajina. We did not receive individual decisions. Or, rather, we as individuals did not receive decisions. It was the president of the municipality that did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And here on the third page of the document we can see the president of the municipality, Dr. Stakic, forwarding this ARK Crisis Staff decision for implementation - correct? - the next day.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, forwarding it to who?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let's go to P2637. I'll ask you a more specific question about its implementation. As you can see, this is a Prijedor SJB document updated the 1st of July, 1992, to the Prijedor Crisis Staff, and it lists a number of conclusions that the SJB is implementing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the very last entry which is on the second page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It states: "The decision of the Banja Luka ARK Crisis Staff, number 03-531 dated the 22nd of June, 1992," and I can tell you that that is the number and date of the ARK Crisis Staff decision we saw a moment ago, "on staffing executive posts and other posts important to the functioning of business establishments has been implemented in this SJB." So, Mr. Mandic, the Prijedor Crisis Staff forwarded the ARK Crisis Staff decision, at the very least, to the SJB, and the SJB here is reporting back to the Crisis Staff of Prijedor that this has been done; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Obviously that's the way it is, but who they replaced, how, what. There were top personnel who also left their work-places and left and those positions had to be filled too, but it doesn't say here who was replaced. They carried out this task, but -- in fact, this is a statement that people were replaced, but who was replaced I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 22 of your statement, you say that during the first few months of the war you did not have contact with the authorities in Pale and that you made all decisions independently. Now, I'd like you to specify, if you could, the time-frame during which you claim you had no contact with the Pale authorities.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I personally did not have any contact whatsoever. I think that it was up until the corridor was created to Bijeljina. Until then, we did not have the possibility of receiving certain orders and instructions as to how we should behave in such complex moments.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So from the beginning of the war until the corridor was created, which the evidence shows was at the very end of June 1992, so I take it that your position is that during the month of May 1992 the Prijedor authorities had no contact with the Pale authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I really cannot give you an answer. I simply don't remember that. I did not have any contacts, and therefore I cannot remember. If it can be seen somewhere that it did exist, if it was written that way, then that's it, but I really cannot remember any of that. And that is my position because I did not go to Pale, I didn't go to Banja Luka. Quite simply, I'm the vice-president. I could not convene sessions of the Executive Board because according to the law I could not do that. It was only the deputy president that could convene sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, your sworn evidence in this case is quite categorical. You say: "After the war began, during the first few months, we in Prijedor did not have contact with the authorities in Pale. We made all decisions independently." Now in your last answer it sounds like you're backtracking from that. You say: I simply don't remember. I did not have any contacts, and therefore I cannot remember. If it can be seen somewhere that it did exist, if it was written that way, then that's it, but I really cannot remember any of that. So what's your evidence on this? Is it what you say in your statement or is it that you just don't know and can't remember?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't think I had any contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have P3919, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now you can see, Mr. Mandic, this is a decision on general public mobilisation of forces and resources in the republic, dated the 20th of May, 1992, issued by the presidency of the RS and signed by Dr. Karadzic. Now, the Prijedor Crisis Staff received and implemented this order; right? Decision, sorry.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Obviously, but I did not receive documents. I can't remember. I apologise to the Court. Documents did not reach me, so I never held this in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P3537, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, this is a decision of the Prijedor Crisis Staff and the preamble says: "Pursuant to the decision of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the general public mobilisation of forces and materiel in the republic, the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality, considering the current situation and conditions, at the meeting held on the 22nd of May, 1992, reached this decision," and the decision on mobilisation follows. Now you -- when I showed you the presidency mobilisation decision from two days previously, you said you didn't remember, Documents did not reach me. I never held this in my hands. Do you remember now that the Prijedor Crisis Staff in fact discussed and implemented that presidency decision at its meeting on the 22nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Obviously the decision was made, but I just simply didn't go anywhere and I didn't -- I don't remember what happened. It's more than 20 years ago. Now I see that that is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P6589, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, these are the minutes of the Prijedor Municipal Board of the SDS meeting held on the 18th of May, 1992, chaired by Mr. Miskovic, and you can see agenda item 2 is report from the session of the Serbian Republic of BH Assembly. And under item 2 in the text it says that a report on the assembly session was presented by President Miskovic, and then there are some notes saying that there were 18 items on the agenda, main guidelines and future activities were identified, commander of the army, supreme staff, appointed, members of the presidency of the republic elected, et cetera. And then it says that the assembly deputy, Svetozar Timarac, presented additional information on this session. Now do you recall this meeting at which Mr. Miskovic and Mr. Timarac reported to the Prijedor SDS on the decisions and discussion at the -- taken at the RS Assembly session from a few days prior to this, on the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, no I can't remember. There were many assembly sessions, really. Sessions of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic and Municipal Board sessions and Crisis Staff sessions, so that -- maybe that was a briefing, information that the commander was elected, the presidency of the republic was elected, but there were other things discussed, too. This was just a briefing, information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, you agree that you were present at this 18th of May session of the Prijedor Municipal Board. We can see you participating in the discussion in item 3.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you have no recollection of any briefing of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: This was a discussion concerning the SDS platform. If there had been any discussion in the previous paragraph, it would have been indicated. But it doesn't mention any discussion. It ended when the president of the party presented what he had to present. Nobody discussed these items on the agenda of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You agree you were present at this session. And one of the -- sorry, the 18th of May session.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. It says so here. It's written. But we didn't discuss.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, one of the items that Mr. Miskovic included in his briefing on the 12th of May are S Assembly session was the main guidelines in future activities. Now, that appears to be a reference to the strategic objectives that Dr. Karadzic announced at the 12th May assembly session. Do you remember Mr. Miskovic telling the Prijedor SDS about the strategic objectives at this SDS session?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly that he spoke. But what he said, I can't remember now. He certainly touched upon some strategic objectives. It's written in the platforms and he must have touched upon these items.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 13 of your statement you say that the Prijedor Crisis Staff established regional staffs to register abandoned property and temporarily accommodated refugees in these properties. Now, you're talking here in your statement about registering abandoned property. In fact, in August of 1992 the Prijedor municipal authorities issued a decision that declared abandoned properties - properties of those who had left the municipality - to be state property; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because somebody had to protect that property. The purpose of regional staffs was to protect property to see which houses were empty, to make a list of things, to keep -- put them in safe keeping, and to provide accommodation for the 60.000 refugees that we already had by that time in Prijedor and these people needed to be put up somewhere. If -- there were people who liked to go around these houses and take whatever they liked, some took off even entire roofs and somebody had to protect these things. Because all the property, all the apartments that belonged to state-owned enterprises were not the property of the person occupying the apartment. It was still social property, public property. It was not the property of an individual but the entire society. That was the law at the time in our country. The only private property was if somebody bought their apartment. The rest was all socially owned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the decision didn't make any distinction between socially owned property and private property. It simply declared abandoned properties to be state properties; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, state property, socially owned property, the same thing. In order to protect it, not in order to re-sell it or to steal it but to protect it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But the municipality didn't have to take over ownership of the properties in order to protect it, did they? They could have simply registered the properties as you claim they did in your statement and allow people to temporarily -- allowed temporarily housing of other -- of refugees, et cetera, in those properties? Declaring those properties to be state properties wasn't required to protect them, was it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know now but I believe that was the legislation at the time. The laws required it. I don't know, I'm not a lawyer. I suppose that the person who made this proposal was guided by the legislation, but I don't know. I cannot really go into these problems. I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this process wasn't just about housing refugees. You were also appropriating business that had been owned previously by Muslims and Croats and issuing them to Serbs for their use; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: There were certain businesses. But now, believe me, there was one company, Hidrofleks, I believe, owned by a Croat, but he had made a contract, an agreement with somebody in Prijedor, a contract on sale. I don't know exactly what happened. I am not familiar with individual cases, so I cannot say whether something was given to a Serb or not. I know about that one case, but apparently a contract on sale was involved. I -- it was not up to me to investigate these things and to inquire.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you're not aware of any other or any business that had been owned by Muslims or Croats where the municipality took over ownership and re-issued those businesses to others for their use? You can't think of a single example?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I am giving you the example of Hidrofleks. I'd like it if you could give me a list here and then I could say item by item. As it is, I can't remember because I was not involved in politics for long at that time. A year before that, I worked in Germany in a German company as the commercial director. I was not interested in these things. I'm not that kind of person. But if you had a list, we could go through the list and say this was taken by that person, this was given to another person, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Mandic, you can't think of a single example of the -- of Prijedor municipality appropriating a business of a Muslim or Croat who had left the municipality and giving it out to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I just thought of one. It's a catering establishment called Cuko, owned by a Muslim, and it was taken over by Dusko Knezevic. I believe he was one of those accused here. But you couldn't stop people like him. He didn't need anybody's permission. He just took what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25827, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is a conclusion of the Prijedor Executive Board dated the 14th of May, 1993. At this point, Mr. Mandic, you were the president of the Executive Board; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, I was vice-president of the Executive Board, but I remember the list. The list is okay. Now I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So at May 1993, Mr. Mandic, you were the president of the Executive Board, were you not? In 1993.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, yes, this is 1993. I thought you were talking about 1992. Yes, I was president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just quickly go to the second page.
