utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think you'll recognise your signature.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is a decision issued and signed by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It states that the -- with the aim of implementing the Executive Board's conclusion of the 22nd of December, 1992, that the immediate family members of soldiers killed in combat and disabled war veterans be awarded 10 commercial premises, the following commercial premises are being selected for that purpose. And then there are a list of ten premises and each one includes the name of the former owner. So the first one is a grocery formerly owned by Dzevad Mujanovic, and it goes on. Now all these ten people identified as former owners of these business, these are all Muslims and Croats, right, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And these business -- you can see, sorry, in item 3 on page 2, it states that all the persons selected to be awarded these business are obliged to sign a commercial property lease contract with the Prijedor municipality. Now, it's clear from this decision that these business were appropriated by the municipality and then awarded to family members of killed soldiers and disabled veterans who were then to enter into a lease contract with the municipality for their use; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago you stated that you could not come up with a single example of the Prijedor municipality appropriating the business of a Muslim or Croat and giving it out to somebody else except for one example where a catering example was taken over by a criminal, Dusko Knezevic, and you said, "... but he didn't need anyone's permission. He just took what he wanted." In fact, Mr. Mandic, the Executive Board of the municipality was doing exactly the same thing as Mr. Knezevic, appropriating business and giving them away -- of non-Serbs and giving them away to Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, these things are not equal. This was done by the authorities and the other thing was done by an individual. An individual is not an authority. This was legal. It was legally decided that this would become state property. It was decided that this property would be protected, and upon a request from the war veteran's association and the families of those who were killed, we assigned these properties to them to have them continue operating and to protect them. Nobody had the right. Nobody could keep these business after the war. The contracts would be terminated and the business returned, so this was legal. Whereas Dusko Knezevic was not in authorities. He was not the state. He could not do these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6606, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 15, Mr. Mandic, you refer to crimes that you call crimes that were blamed on the Serbian people, and you say that: "It is generally known that various individual murders happened and that police organs and the prosecutor's office of Prijedor municipality undertook various investigations and filed misdemeanor and criminal reports against known or unknown perpetrators." Now which individual murders, as you put it, of non-Serbs in 1992 are you aware of?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I'll give you an example. I believe it was the Rizvanovic family, he was a car mechanic. And I believe the other family's name is Dosen. He committed the murder by night. I don't know exactly, but I believe it was very -- I mean, fear pervaded Prijedor. We all knew this man by sight, and the moment he drank a bit he lost control completely and then what happened happened. I believe the police station carried out an on-site investigation and identified the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And who was the perpetrator of this incident, of this murder?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: A person whose nickname was Djole. Rumor had it it was him. I did not have any documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And was this person whose -- with whom -- about whom you only know the nickname, was that person prosecuted by the Republika Srpska authorities at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a matter for the prosecutor's office and the police, so --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for a clarification? I'm not sure that the witness knows only the person's nickname. I believe that he also mentioned his family name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the man's family name was Dosen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Any other cases of what you call individual murders that you are specifically aware of of non-Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, it was during war operations, during conflicts, during the attack on Prijedor. But I suppose all was documented and that the actors are known and those were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you just said -- you've only named one case of an individual of a murder that you're aware of, you don't know if the perpetrator was prosecuted, and now you say: "I suppose all was documented and the actors are known ..." So in your statement when you said police organs in the prosecutor's office of the Prijedor municipality undertook various investigations and filed misdemeanors and criminal reports against perpetrators, what exactly is that based on if you can only name one murder incident and you don't even know if the perpetrator was prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that everybody did what they were supposed to do, that courts and the prosecutor's office did what they were supposed to and the police did the same. One couldn't just turn a blind eye on events that happened because they did happen, and I suppose that they documented those things and that they caught the perpetrators. There were talks about various people who had done things. I didn't go to the police or to the court to ask whether they followed through or not and who the perps were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said one couldn't just turn a blind eye on events that happened because they did happen. Now, you were, in 1992, a member of the Crisis Staff. You were vice-president of the Executive Committee. And in 1993 you were president of the Executive Committee. Did either of these organs, the Crisis Staff or Executive Committee, take any steps to investigate or gather information about crimes against Muslims and Croats in 1992 while you were members of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I believe so. I think so. I believe that what happened in Keraterm resulted in the trial of the persons who were involved. I'm assuming that there are records of on-site investigations by the police. I can only share with you my assumptions because I had never saw any documents. However, if they were doing their job, then they must have documented those things and they must have arrested the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic, you may have misunderstood my question. I'm asking you about the bodies that you belonged to: The Crisis Staff and the Executive Committee of Prijedor. Did those bodies take any steps to gather information about the crimes committed against Muslims and Croats in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, the Executive Board was operational for the first ten days after the take-over, and then it was the Crisis Staff that took over. When the Crisis Staff was abolished, the Executive Board continued operating. I believe that at a meeting we decided that we should investigate crimes committed against the Serb population in Prijedor municipality and that we were in communication with Minister Toholj, I believe that that was his name, and Mr. Bolajic as well, who lived in Belgrade and who was affiliated with the United Nations and worked on crime investigation. While I was the president of the Executive Board there was that one attempt to investigate some of the crimes that were committed against Serbs in Prijedor municipality. And as for the rest, I don't know. We did not investigate anything during my term of office.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25829, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in your last answer you talked about a decision taken by the Executive Board to investigate crimes committed against the Serb population, and you refer to communication with Minister Toholj in that regard. And here we see a letter authored by you to Mr. Toholj dated the 7th of May, 1993, stating that the Executive Committee of Prijedor municipality had formed a municipal commission for gathering documents on the genocide committed against the Serbian people in the territory of our municipality. And it goes on to talk about efforts to obtain documentation and requests the minister to facilitate the commission's efforts to gather documents and information with the Ministry of Defence and minister of the interior. Now, this letter reflects the efforts you referred to a moment ago by the Prijedor Executive Board to investigate crimes against Serbs in Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor explain whether the collection of documentation is tantamount to investigation, or whether she considers it to be investigation?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Those were the witness's own words in the previous long answer. I tender this document and I have no further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6607, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, will you start your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, since we have to work tomorrow perhaps it would be best if I could start tomorrow. We have only five minutes left and if you want me to, I can make the most of the five minutes that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tomorrow, but we'll begin with Mr. Beara's evidence, as far as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's better not to start because the few times we'll be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that means you have more than 10 or 15 minutes for your re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But no more than 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will consult my colleagues. If you could conclude in 15 minutes, why don't we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just let me consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that we started earlier than usual for this session, if the interpreters are fine with this arrangement, we'll continue with their indulgence, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you conclude by five to 3.00? In 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I hope so. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic, in the document that is before us, it says: "Collection of documents." On page 96, you were asked whether the Crisis Staff, and later on the Executive Board, took any measures to investigate crimes. Could you please tell us whether a Crisis Staff or an Executive Board have their own investigative bodies which are not the regular investigation bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, neither crisis staff nor an Executive Board have their own investigating bodies. There is the police, the court, and those are the bodies that belong to the powers of the state that have the authority to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the Crisis Staff or the Executive Board, did they have any authority over the judiciary or was the division of powers present and respected in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Everybody did their job. The court did what it was supposed to, the police as well, so there was a division of powers between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 95, you were asked why you remembered only one case of murder. Could you tell us whether in the area outside of combat activities, there were more killings of Serbs than others in general terms?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that there were, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many? Could you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, not that many in that sense. There were such cases but I can't remember any details. I remembered that particular case because I live downtown and I remember that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on page 92 you were asked about the take-over of property by the municipality. Could you please tell us whether the take-over of property means that the ownership is also taken over? And how many units of private property actually changed hands or changed the ownership in an illegal way in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to answer that question because people entered houses and they did whatever they wanted. However, things had to be channeled. And if somebody entered the house, it had to be known that they live there, that they had to behave like good hosts, that they had to protect the property. They were not supposed to live in one house for a while and then in another next, so commissions were set up to make stock of that property so as to allow the municipality to give the available property to refugees and displaced persons with the help of the commissions that were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about property in war? When somebody disposes or gets property at their disposal, do they also get ownership of that property? And how many pieces of property did the state take over as its property?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't happen. It never -- the state never registered as the owner. The ownership remained the same but the deeds were not changed, is what I'm saying. If Marko Markovic was the owner of a house he was still the owner, but the state was the custodian of such property because the owner -- the rightful owner was not there. It was done in order to protect property. There were no books of empty properties where such properties would be registered in the land books or in the registry books. There was a state of chaos -- or chaos prevailed and empty property had to be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I receive an apartment from one company and then I leave that company, whereas the apartment belongs to the company, whose -- in whose ownership is it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: The apartment remains in the -- is in the ownership of the company, and if you leave the company you have to return the apartment. That's the law. By living in the apartment, you do not get property rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from these private businesses, we're talking now about socially owned companies, whose ownership is it, in fact, when we say "socially owned"?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: It's owned by all the citizens, the society as a whole. Nobody can say that they own the company. That was the system in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about communications.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show D01832, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by your assertion that communications were compromised, that it was difficult to establish contact?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a member of the State Security Service, well known to us by his code-name. Can you read what is written in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: Shall I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, aloud.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: "The situation is difficult. Communications are broken down. In Prijedor, yesterday, a reservist policeman of Serb nationality was killed from behind. Immediately after, a relative of the dead policeman killed four Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed this entire question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked: How is this consistent with your experience from Prijedor from that time concerning communications, revenge, murders, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I answered "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated] On page 73, you were asked -- the question was -- I'll read in English: [In English] "As a result of the night between 29th and 30th of April, 1992, following very detailed preparations and pursuant to the relevant decisions of the Executive Committee for the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, an organised take-over of power was embarked upon." [Interpretation] And then further on: [In English] "And now as this police report makes clear, this take-over by the SDS in Prijedor was planned long before the telex was received ...," [Interpretation] and so on. Your answer was: [In English] "Yes, but that was not the only reason. I mean the Cazin Krajina." [Interpretation] Can you tell us what were the other reasons? What made the authorities carry out preparations for some contingency?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand if you cited the telegram by the minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Delimustafic, which was the spark that provoked this take-over of power?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the take-over. A passage was read out to you from a MUP report saying that these preparations had been conducted earlier and the telegram only speeded up the take-over. According to the Law on All People's Defence and for practical reasons, do the authorities always make such contingency preparations?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC
utterances.text: This just provided a cause. It was not only that Cazin Krajina you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He didn't get the answer he wanted the first time and now he's asking it again in an incredibly leading manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said he didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was because you didn't cite sufficiently for the witness to understand what the question was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I'm in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But here, you were shown a police report saying that contingency preparations had been made earlier, and you --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- answered --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The report doesn't say that contingency preparations had been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The report says: "Activities were launched to prepare for a take-over by force." The report also mentions the Cazin Krajina -- it may assist the witness if Dr. Karadzic go -- if he wants to ask about that particular aspect to go to the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the question and answer will be -- I will read those parts to you. The question is this: "Now as this police report makes clear, this take-over by the SDS in Prijedor was planned long before the telex was received on the 29th of April; correct?" And this is your answer: "Yes. But that was not the only reason. I mean, the Cazin Krajina." So then, Mr. Karadzic was asking what are the other reasons that you had in mind? Can you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party was involved in intensive negotiations with the leadership of the SDA about a peaceful solution to all the interethnic issues in Prijedor. The Serbian Democratic Party was very committed to finding a peaceful solution, keeping the peace, and it wanted the removal of extremists among the SDA members, people who were already known in Prijedor -- or better to call them notorious such as one Hadzija and one man named Ecimovic and we had information that they were already distributing arms around villages. I live in a place that is close to a Muslim village, so I could see with my own eyes how they were walking about the hills. So we had to protect the Serbian people, but not only the Serbian people, the Muslim people as well because God forbid that Muslims should have taken over power in Prijedor. We had a very bad experience from the Second World War. But under the previous system in which we lived, it was forbidden to talk about these things. However, after Tito's death and the democratic changes, our people learned much more about who had done what and who was doing what. So we tried in a peaceful way, and we, the Serbian people, I believe managed to save many, many more lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber doesn't want to obliged you to conclude your re-examination being pressed for time. We'll continue tomorrow, if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Better to continue tomorrow, then, because we've lost some time in these misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we'll continue tomorrow. Unfortunately, we are not able to finish your examination. But tomorrow we'll begin with Mr. Beara's cross-examination. I don't know how much time it will -- it will be necessary to conclude his evidence. You'll be heard after Mr. Beara's evidence is concluded. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your kind understanding. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- do not discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving evidence. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.
